subject: civil
audience: FE Civil candidates and civil engineering students
title: The Tank Gauge That Read 58.9 kPa at 6 m
featured_title: THE TANK GAUGE THAT READ 58.9 KPA AT 6 M

presentation.challenge: The water was motionless, but pressure still increased with depth.

practice.primary_question: Why does gauge pressure in a static liquid increase linearly with depth?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Treating pressure in a static liquid as uniform with depth because the fluid velocity is zero.

case_dna.target_misconception: If water is not moving, gauge pressure is the same everywhere in the tank.
case_dna.why_plausible: Zero velocity means no dynamic pressure change from motion, which can be confused with zero hydrostatic gradient.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: For water, p=rho g h. At h=6 m, p=1000×9.81×6=58,860 Pa=58.9 kPa gauge.
case_dna.corrected_model: In a static incompressible liquid, gauge pressure increases with vertical depth according to p=rho g h.

problem_statement: An open water tank has a pressure tap 6 m below the free surface. A technician expects near-zero gauge pressure because the water is stationary. The gauge reads about 58.9 kPa. Calculate the hydrostatic gauge pressure and identify the mistaken assumption.
fixed_constraints: Tap depth = 6 m below an atmospheric free surface

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The water was still. The pressure was not zero.
gates.prompt: What creates pressure when the fluid has no velocity?

options.label: Gauge pressure is p=rho g h below an atmospheric free surface
options.reason: The weight of the liquid column creates the hydrostatic pressure.

options.label: Pressure is zero because velocity is zero
options.reason: Zero velocity removes dynamic effects, not hydrostatic pressure.

options.label: Pressure is uniform throughout the water because the tank is open
options.reason: Only the free-surface pressure equals atmospheric; pressure increases with depth.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the gauge pressure
gates.prompt: At 6 m depth in water, what gauge pressure do you expect?

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the hydrostatic pressure
gates.prompt: Use p=rho g h with rho=1000 kg/m^3, g=9.81 m/s^2, h=6 m. Enter p in kPa.
gates.hint: Divide pascals by 1000 to convert to kPa.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: Depth, not velocity, explains the reading

cards.text: The free surface is exposed to atmospheric pressure.
Gauge pressure increases by rho g for each meter of depth.
At 6 m, rho g h = 58.86 kPa.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the tank-pressure note
report: C1. The tank is open to atmosphere.
C3. Therefore gauge pressure is zero at every depth.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: Static fluid still has a hydrostatic pressure gradient.

evidence_choices.label: p=rho g h=58.86 kPa at 6 m
evidence_choices.reason: This directly predicts the measured gauge pressure.

correction.template: At 6 m depth, the hydrostatic gauge pressure is about {pressure} kPa.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Reduce gauge pressure at the tap
gates.constraint: Keep the tank open and the same liquid.

options.label: Move the tap to a shallower depth
options.reason: Hydrostatic pressure is directly proportional to depth.

options.label: Increase the tank plan area without changing depth
options.reason: Hydrostatic pressure at a point depends on depth and fluid density, not tank plan area.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the hydrostatic rule
gates.prompt: Approximately what gauge pressure exists 3 m below a water surface?

options.label: 9.81 kPa
options.reason: That corresponds to only 1 m of water.

options.label: 0 kPa
options.reason: Only the open free surface is at zero gauge pressure.

gates.explanation: For water, hydrostatic gauge pressure increases about 9.81 kPa per meter of depth.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the fluid-statics model
gates.confirmation: I confirm that a static liquid can have nonzero gauge pressure due to the weight of the liquid above the point.

items.label: What failed
items.value: Static fluid was incorrectly treated as zero-pressure fluid.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: The weight of the water column creates a pressure gradient.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Use p=rho g h for gauge pressure below an atmospheric free surface.

seo.seo_title: Hydrostatic Pressure at 6 m Depth: 58.9 kPa | FE Civil E-047
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Civil Case E-047: water at 6 m depth has about 58.9 kPa gauge pressure even when the fluid is stationary.
seo.excerpt: Zero velocity does not mean zero pressure. A static water column develops pressure that increases with depth.
seo.direct_answer: In a static liquid beneath an atmospheric free surface, gauge pressure is p=rho g h. For water at 6 m depth, p=1000×9.81×6=58.86 kPa gauge.

faqs.q: What is water pressure at 6 m depth?
Does hydrostatic pressure depend on tank area?
faqs.a: No. At a given depth it depends on fluid density, gravity, and depth.
